3	\section{Finite optimization and checks on review arguments}
4	\label{S:nogo-optimization}
5	
6	The last group concerns finite calculations. These examples are small enough
7	that every number can be checked directly, but the distinctions they expose
8	matter in the infinite-dimensional proof: the two variance directions, the
9	normalization of an energy, the active set of an optimization, and the exact
10	inequality used in a review.
11	
12	\subsection{NG-23: both Gaussian variance directions}
13	\label{S:nogo-23}
14	
15	A rectangular Gaussian matrix has an input variance and an output variance.
16	Keeping only one would simplify the moment estimate, but the dimensions of
17	the two spaces cannot be ignored. This is the counterexample behind
18	Remark~\ref{R:gaussian-one-variance-test}.
19	
20	\setcounter{nogo}{22}
21	\begin{nogo}[A one-sided variance bound fails]\label{P:nogo-23}
22	  Let $g_1,\ldots,g_n$ be independent standard real Gaussians,
23	  $A_i=e_i^{\mathsf T}$ the coordinate row matrices, and
24	  $X=\sum_i g_iA_i$. Put $V_{\rm in}=\sum_iA_i^*A_i$ and
25	  $V_{\rm out}=\sum_iA_iA_i^*$. For $n=16$,
26	  \[
27	    \E\|X\|_{S_4}^4=288>144=9\operatorname{Tr}V_{\rm in}^2.
28	  \]
29	  The transposed family gives the analogous failure of an output-only bound.
30	  More generally, no constant independent of $n$ bounds the left side by
31	  $\operatorname{Tr}V_{\rm in}^2$ alone for all these row matrices.
32	\end{nogo}
33	
34	\begin{proof}
35	  The only nonzero singular value of $X$ is
36	  $(\sum_i g_i^2)^{1/2}$. Since $\E g_i^4=3$ and
37	  $\E g_i^2g_j^2=1$ for $i\ne j$,
38	  \[
39	    \E\|X\|_{S_4}^4
40	    =\E\left(\sum_i g_i^2\right)^2
41	    =3n+n(n-1)=n(n+2).
42	  \]
43	  Here $V_{\rm in}=I_n$, whereas $V_{\rm out}=n$ acts on a
44	  one-dimensional space. The proposed bound gives $9n$, which is smaller
45	  than $n(n+2)$ at $n=16$. The ratio to $\operatorname{Tr}V_{\rm in}^2=n$
46	  is $n+2$, so no fixed constant works for all $n$. Transposition exchanges
47	  the variance directions and preserves the singular values. This proves
48	  No-go~\ref{P:nogo-23}.
49	\end{proof}
50	
51	\paragraph{Scope and what survives.}
52	This is a finite-matrix counterexample, not a counterexample to a wave
53	estimate. Proposition~\ref{P:finite-gaussian-matrix} retains both variances.
54	At $n=16$, its average and maximum bounds have fourth powers $1224$ and
55	$2304$, respectively, and neither is contradicted by $288$.
56	
57	\paragraph{What would permit a different estimate?}
58	A one-sided estimate would need additional structure relating the two
59	variance operators, with its dimension dependence stated. It cannot follow
60	from the Gaussian matrix form alone.

62	\subsection{NG-28: the normalization matters when bounds are compared}
63	\label{S:nogo-28}
64	
65	The occupation argument gives the upper ceiling $U_2$ for $C_2$.
66	It is tempting to compare it with an energy expression by changing the
67	coefficient of the gradient penalty. The comparison must be calculated:
68	a value with penalty one is not interchangeable with a value with penalty
69	one-half. In particular, not every comparison value below is itself a proved
70	upper bound for the moment constant.
71	
72	Retain $q=4-\alpha$, $k=3-\alpha$ and $m=q/k$, and the occupation energies
73	$\mathcal{E}_\zeta^{\mathcal O}$ of~\eqref{E:raw-occupation-definitions}.
74	For $z>0$, the scalar maps are
75	\[
76	  F_b(z)=k\left[
77	  \frac{(q-2b)^{(q-2b)/2}}{8(q-b)^{q-b}}
78	  \left(\frac{2z}{2-\alpha}\right)^{(2-\alpha)/2}
79	  \right]^{1/k},\qquad 0\le b<q/2.
80	\]
81	These are the maps in~\eqref{E:occupation-scalar-map}; here $b$ is only
82	a display parameter and $a=\alpha_0$ is the temporal exponent.
83	
84	\setcounter{nogo}{27}
85	\begin{nogo}[An occupation ceiling need not improve a comparison value]
86	  \label{P:nogo-28}
87	  For $d=2$, $\alpha=5/4$, $a=1/2$ and every nonzero admissible covariance,
88	  \[
89	    2^mF_a(\mathcal{E}_1^{\mathcal O})<U_2.
90	  \]
91	  Thus, the reverse comparison is not valid throughout the admissible class.
92	\end{nogo}
93	
94	\begin{proof}
95	  The energies are finite and positive by
96	  Proposition~\ref{P:raw-occupation-energy}. Put
97	  \[
98	    \Delta=\frac12\{q\log q+(q-2a)\log(q-2a)\}
99	    -(q-a)\log(q-a).
100	  \]
101	  Subtracting the logarithms of $F_a$ and $F_0$ gives
102	  $\log(F_a(z)/F_0(z))=\Delta/k$. The identity in
103	  Theorem~\ref{T:intrinsic-occupation-ceiling} gives
104	  $U_2=2^m(2\zeta)^{\alpha/(2k)}F_0(\mathcal{E}_\zeta^{\mathcal O})$.
105	  Therefore,
106	  \[
107	    \frac{2^mF_a(\mathcal{E}_\zeta^{\mathcal O})}{U_2}
108	    =\exp\left\{\frac{\Delta-(\alpha/2)\log(2\zeta)}{k}\right\}.
109	  \]
110	  At the stated parameters, $q=11/4$, $k=7/4$, and
111	  \[
112	    8\{\Delta-(\alpha/2)\log2\}
113	    =\log\frac{11^{11}7^7}{2^5 9^{18}}<0,
114	  \]
115	  because
116	  \[
117	    234966429149994773<4803028329503971872.
118	  \]
119	  This proves No-go~\ref{P:nogo-28}.
120	\end{proof}
121	
122	\paragraph{Scope and what survives.}
123	This refutes an ordering of two computed quantities, not an inequality for
124	the actual moment. It does not decide whether $C_2$ is below the smaller
125	comparison value. At $\zeta=1/2$, the logarithmic difference is instead
126	$\Delta/k>0$, by strict convexity of $x\log x$; that is the valid strict
127	comparison in Corollary~\ref{C:intrinsic-spatial-bracket}.
128	
129	\paragraph{What would permit a different comparison?}
130	Match the covariance amplitude, admissible profiles and kinetic penalty,
131	then prove the sign of the resulting ratio in the parameter range claimed.
132	Comparing the names of the energies is insufficient.
133	
134	\subsection{NG-29: three safeguards in the Gram optimization}
135	\label{S:nogo-29}
136	
137	The finite optimization of Section~\ref{S:finite-positive-gram} uses
138	\[
139	  F(\Phi)=2\sum_i\ell_i
140	  \sqrt{(\langle\Phi,k_i\rangle-b_i)_+}-\frac12\|\Phi\|^2,
141	  \qquad \ell_i>0,\quad b_i\ge0.
142	\]
143	The Gram entries $C_{ij}=\langle k_i,k_j\rangle$ are nonnegative. Three
144	possible simplifications fail: omitting the empty active set, invoking
145	global concavity, and treating entrywise order as positive semidefinite order.
146	
147	\setcounter{nogo}{28}
148	\begin{nogo}[Empty sets, concavity and matrix order]\label{P:nogo-29}
149	  Each of the following failures occurs within the finite setting above.
150	  \begin{enumerate}
151	    \item With one unit vector, $\ell=1/10$ and $b=4$, the nonempty-set
152	      dual infimum is negative, while the primal supremum is nonnegative.
153	    \item With $H=\R$ and $k=\ell=b=1$, the primal objective is not concave.
154	    \item There are positive semidefinite Grams $C,D$ with
155	      $0\le C_{ij}\le D_{ij}$ for every entry but $D-C$ not positive semidefinite.
156	  \end{enumerate}
157	\end{nogo}
158	
159	\begin{proof}
160	  In the first example the nonempty dual is
161	  \[
162	    D(w)=\frac{1}{100w}-4w+\frac{w^2}{2},\qquad w>0.
163	  \]
164	  Its infimum is at most $D(4)=-3199/400<0$, whereas $F(0)=0$.
165	  Dropping the empty value from the maximum of dual infima therefore cannot
166	  give the primal supremum.
167	
168	  In the second example $F(x)=2\sqrt{(x-1)_+}-x^2/2$. Directly,
169	  $F(0)=F(2)=0$ but $F(1)=-1/2$, violating midpoint concavity.
170	
171	  For the third example take
172	  \[
173	    C=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
174	    D=\begin{pmatrix}1&1/2\\1/2&1\end{pmatrix}.
175	  \]
176	  The eigenvalues of $D$ are $3/2$ and $1/2$, while those of $D-C$ are
177	  $1/2$ and $-1/2$. All entries are ordered as claimed. This proves
178	  No-go~\ref{P:nogo-29}.
179	\end{proof}
180	
181	\paragraph{Scope and what survives.}
182	These are the checks in Remark~\ref{R:gram-controls}. They explain the
183	empty-set convention and active-set proof of
184	Proposition~\ref{P:gram-positive-optimizer}. Entrywise comparison still
185	works in Proposition~\ref{P:gram-entrywise-comparison}: for nonnegative
186	weights $w_i$, the form $\sum_{i,j}w_i(D_{ij}-C_{ij})w_j$ is nonnegative.
187	No order on all vectors, and no covariance monotonicity for nonlinear waves,
188	is asserted by that calculation.
189	
190	\paragraph{What would permit a shortcut?}
191	A restricted concavity argument must first justify its active region.
192	A matrix comparison must specify the vectors on which its quadratic form
193	is nonnegative. Neither step follows from a convenient change of terminology.

195	\subsection{NG-33: check the mathematics returned by a reviewer}
196	\label{S:nogo-33}
197	
198	A review report is also a mathematical argument and can contain an incorrect
199	step. This historical record groups three such checks. The manuscript had
200	the correct expressions; the examples below explain why the proposed review
201	steps could not replace them. These are not three new counterexamples to the
202	stochastic model.
203	
204	\setcounter{nogo}{32}
205	\begin{nogo}[Three invalid proof steps]\label{P:nogo-33}
206	  The following assertions fail.
207	  \begin{enumerate}
208	    \item The free phase matrix
209	      $S_0(t)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&t\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$
210	      is a contraction in the Euclidean norm for every $t\ge0$.
211	    \item For $0<\vartheta<1$, the series term $x^n/(n!)^\vartheta$ equals
212	      $A_nB_n$, where
213	      \[
214	        A_n=\frac{(2x^{1/\vartheta})^n}{n!},\qquad
215	        B_n=2^{-\vartheta n/(1-\vartheta)}.
216	      \]
217	    \item The denominator $k!\,k^{(2-\alpha)k}$ may always be replaced by
218	      the larger denominator $(k!)^3$ in the coefficient bound of
219	      Proposition~\ref{P:low-alpha-upper}.
220	  \end{enumerate}
221	\end{nogo}
222	
223	\begin{proof}
224	  The vector $(0,1)$ has norm one, but its image under $S_0(t)$ has norm
225	  $\sqrt{1+t^2}>1$ for $t>0$. The same obstruction applies to the normalized
226	  whole-space wave phase: its Fourier matrix tends to $S_0(t)$ as
227	  $|\xi|\to0$. Unit Fourier bumps concentrated near zero, placed in the
228	  velocity coordinate, therefore have image norms tending to
229	  $\sqrt{1+t^2}$. The valid estimate keeps an exponential free-growth factor.
230	
231	  The correct identity in the second assertion is
232	  $x^n/(n!)^\vartheta=A_n^\vartheta B_n^{1-\vartheta}$.
233	  At $\vartheta=3/4$, $n=1$ and $x=1$, its left side is one, whereas
234	  $A_1B_1=2\cdot(1/8)=1/4$. H\"older applies to the weighted product, as
235	  in the proof of Proposition~\ref{P:static-phase-all-orders}.
236	
237	  For the third assertion choose the permitted spatial-white value
238	  $\alpha=1$ and $k=3$. Then $k!k^{(2-\alpha)k}=162<216=(k!)^3$.
239	  An upper bound $M/162$ does not imply the smaller upper bound $M/216$.
240	  The valid factorial weakening is instead
241	  \[
242	    k!k^{(2-\alpha)k}\ge(k!)^{3-\alpha},
243	  \]
244	  since $k!\le k^k$ and $2-\alpha>0$; at this example its right side is
245	  $36$. This proves No-go~\ref{P:nogo-33}.
246	\end{proof}
247	
248	\paragraph{Scope and what survives.}
249	The last arithmetic check refutes an inference between numerical bounds;
250	it does not prove that the actual coefficient exceeds $M/216$.
251	All three corrected arguments remain in the main text. Their lesson is to
252	check an asserted derivation against its domains, factors and quantifiers,
253	even when the report containing it has a favorable overall verdict.
254	
255	\paragraph{What would permit the discarded steps?}
256	Contractivity needs a suitable invariant norm or a restricted state class.
257	The H\"older factors need their conjugate powers. A stronger factorial
258	bound needs an additional estimate; it cannot be obtained by changing the
259	exponent in the denominator.

4	\section{Finite optimization with nonnegative Gram entries}
5	\label{S:finite-positive-gram}
6	
7	Let $H$ be any real Hilbert space, $\mathcal{I}$ a finite index set, $k_i \in
8	H$, $\ell_i > 0$ and $b_i \ge 0$. Write $C_{ij} = \langle k_i,k_j\rangle$ and
9	assume $C_{ij} \ge 0$ for every pair. The Gram matrix is symmetric and positive
10	semidefinite, since $\sum_{i,j}a_iC_{ij}a_j = \|\sum_i a_i k_i\|^2$. Put $t_+ =
11	\max(t,0)$ and define
12	\begin{equation}\label{E:finite-gram-score}
13	  \mathfrak{F}_C(\Phi)
14	  =2\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\ell_i
15	  \sqrt{(\langle\Phi,k_i\rangle-b_i)_+}-\|\Phi\|^2/2,
16	  \qquad \mathscr{S}(C)=\sup_{\Phi\in H}\mathfrak{F}_C(\Phi).
17	\end{equation}
18	Let $\mathcal{J} = \{i:k_i\ne0\} = \{i:C_{ii}>0\}$. Zero vectors contribute zero
19	because $b_i \ge 0$. Empty index sets, singular Grams and $H = \{0\}$ are
20	allowed. For nonempty $A \subset \mathcal{J}$ and $w_i > 0$, set
21	\begin{equation}\label{E:finite-gram-dual}
22	  D_A^C(w)=\sum_{i\in A}\frac{\ell_i^2}{w_i}
23	  -\sum_{i\in A}b_iw_i
24	  +\frac12\sum_{i,j\in A}w_iC_{ij}w_j,
25	  \qquad d_A^C=\inf_{w_i>0}D_A^C(w).
26	\end{equation}
27	Set $d_\varnothing^C = 0$.
28	
29	\begin{lemma}[Scalar and Hilbert identities]\label{L:gram-scalar-algebra}
30	  For real $\ell$, $w > 0$ and $t \ge 0$,
31	  \begin{equation}\label{E:gram-sqrt-dual}
32	    2\ell\sqrt t\le\ell^2/w+wt.
33	  \end{equation}
34	  For $\Phi,z \in H$,
35	  \begin{equation}\label{E:gram-hilbert-square}
36	    \langle\Phi,z\rangle-\|\Phi\|^2/2
37	    =\|z\|^2/2-\|\Phi-z\|^2/2\le\|z\|^2/2.
38	  \end{equation}
39	  For finite real $w_i$, $\|\sum_iw_ik_i\|^2 = \sum_{i,j}w_iC_{ij}w_j$.
40	\end{lemma}
41	
42	\begin{proof}
43	  Since $\sqrt w > 0$ and $\sqrt{wt} = \sqrt w\sqrt t$,
44	  \[
45	    0\le(\ell/\sqrt w-\sqrt{wt})^2
46	    =\ell^2/w+wt-2\ell\sqrt t.
47	  \]
48	  This includes $t = 0$. If $\ell,t > 0$, equality holds for $w = \ell/\sqrt t$.
49	  Expanding $\|\Phi-z\|^2$ proves~\eqref{E:gram-hilbert-square}. Bilinearity of
50	  the real inner product proves the finite Gram identity. These identities use
51	  neither compactness of a Hilbert ball nor an inverse covariance matrix. This
52	  proves Lemma~\ref{L:gram-scalar-algebra}.
53	\end{proof}
54	
55	\begin{lemma}[Interior dual minimum]\label{L:gram-dual-minimum}
56	  Each nonempty $A \subset \mathcal{J}$ has a unique positive minimizer $w^A$ of
57	  $D_A^C$. At this minimizer,
58	  \begin{equation}\label{E:gram-dual-stationarity}
59	    \sum_{j\in A}C_{ij}w_j^A-b_i
60	    =\frac{\ell_i^2}{(w_i^A)^2}>0,\qquad i\in A.
61	  \end{equation}
62	\end{lemma}
63	
64	\begin{proof}
65	  Put $c_i = C_{ii} > 0$ and $K_A = \sum_{i\in A}b_i^2/c_i$. Nonnegative entries
66	  and positive weights give
67	  \[
68	    D_A^C(w)\ge
69	    \sum_i\left(\ell_i^2/w_i-b_iw_i+c_iw_i^2/2\right).
70	  \]
71	  Completing the square in $c_iw_i^2/4-b_iw_i$ yields
72	  \begin{equation}\label{E:gram-dual-coercivity}
73	    D_A^C(w)\ge
74	    \sum_i\ell_i^2/w_i+\frac14\sum_i c_iw_i^2-K_A.
75	  \end{equation}
76	  Thus, no coordinate can approach zero or infinity in a bounded sublevel while
77	  a different negative term hides its growth. Take $w^0 = (1,\ldots,1)$, $d_0 =
78	  D_A^C(w^0)$ and $L_A = d_0+K_A$. Equation~\eqref{E:gram-dual-coercivity} at
79	  $w^0$ gives $L_A \ge \sum_i\ell_i^2+\sum_i c_i/4 > 0$. Every $w$ with
80	  $D_A^C(w) \le d_0$ satisfies
81	  \[
82	    \ell_i^2/L_A\le w_i\le\sqrt{4L_A/c_i}.
83	  \]
84	  The sublevel is nonempty and closed inside this compact box, which lies in the
85	  open positive orthant. A minimizing sequence chosen in the sublevel has a
86	  convergent subsequence there. Continuity attains its infimum. Outside this
87	  sublevel the values exceed $d_0$, so the minimum is global on the entire
88	  positive orthant.
89	
90	  The function is smooth in that orthant. Its Hessian on a nonzero vector $\xi$
91	  has value
92	  \[
93	    \sum_i\frac{2\ell_i^2}{w_i^3}\xi_i^2
94	    +\sum_{i,j}\xi_iC_{ij}\xi_j>0.
95	  \]
96	  The first term is strictly positive and the second is a squared Hilbert norm.
97	  Restriction to any nonconstant line segment is strictly convex, proving
98	  uniqueness. Each coordinate permits both signs of a small perturbation at the
99	  interior minimum. Differentiation gives $-\ell_i^2/w_i^2-b_i+\sum_jC_{ij}w_j =
100	  0$. This is~\eqref{E:gram-dual-stationarity}. This proves
101	  Lemma~\ref{L:gram-dual-minimum}.
102	\end{proof}
103	
104	\begin{proposition}[Positive conic maximizer]\label{P:gram-positive-optimizer}
105	  The finite real value in~\eqref{E:finite-gram-score} satisfies
106	  \begin{equation}\label{E:gram-active-duality}
107	    \mathscr{S}(C)=\max_{A\subset\mathcal{J}}d_A^C .
108	  \end{equation}
109	  If a maximizing subset is empty, $\Phi = 0$ attains the supremum. If a
110	  maximizing subset $A$ is nonempty, a maximizer is $\Phi_A = \sum_{i\in A}w_i^A
111	  k_i$ with strictly positive coefficients. No uniqueness of the primal
112	  maximizer or maximizing subset is asserted.
113	\end{proposition}
114	
115	\begin{proof}
116	  For arbitrary $\Phi$, let $A(\Phi) = \{i:\langle\Phi,k_i\rangle>b_i\}$. It is
117	  contained in $\mathcal{J}$. All other terms in the objective vanish, including
118	  equality at the threshold. If $A(\Phi)$ is empty, $\mathfrak{F}_C(\Phi) =
119	  -\|\Phi\|^2/2 \le 0$. Otherwise, for any positive $w$ on $A = A(\Phi)$, set
120	  $t_i = \langle\Phi,k_i\rangle-b_i > 0$ and $z = \sum_{i\in A}w_ik_i$.
121	  Lemma~\ref{L:gram-scalar-algebra} gives
122	  \[
123	    \mathfrak{F}_C(\Phi)
124	    \le\sum_i\ell_i^2/w_i-\sum_i b_iw_i
125	    +\langle\Phi,z\rangle-\|\Phi\|^2/2
126	    \le D_A^C(w).
127	  \]
128	  This holds for every positive $w$, so $\mathfrak{F}_C(\Phi) \le d_A^C$. There
129	  are finitely many subsets and their values are finite by
130	  Lemma~\ref{L:gram-dual-minimum}. Taking the supremum bounds $\mathscr{S}(C)$
131	  above by their maximum.
132	
133	  Conversely, $\mathfrak{F}_C(0) = 0 = d_\varnothing^C$. For nonempty $A$, take
134	  its dual minimizer. Equation~\eqref{E:gram-dual-stationarity} makes every
135	  vector in $A$ strictly active at $\Phi_A$, with
136	  $\sqrt{\langle\Phi_A,k_i\rangle-b_i} = \ell_i/w_i^A$. Both inequalities in the
137	  preceding display are then equalities for the sum restricted to $A$, since $z
138	  = \Phi_A$. This restricted objective equals $d_A^C$. All omitted vectors
139	  contribute nonnegative terms to the full objective, hence
140	  $\mathfrak{F}_C(\Phi_A) \ge d_A^C$, even if this value is negative. Maximizing
141	  over $A$, including the empty set, proves \eqref{E:gram-active-duality} and
142	  the asserted attainment. For a maximizing nonempty subset the upper and lower
143	  bounds force $\mathfrak{F}_C(\Phi_A) = d_A^C$; no outside inactivity was
144	  assumed. All-zero vectors give $\mathscr{S}(C) = 0$ directly. This proves
145	  Proposition~\ref{P:gram-positive-optimizer}.
146	\end{proof}
147	
148	No-go~\ref{P:nogo-29} gives the three finite counterexamples behind this
149	formulation: the empty active set cannot be omitted, the primal objective
150	need not be concave, and entrywise matrix order is not positive
151	semidefinite order.

158	\begin{lemma}[Real Gram realization]\label{L:gram-realization}
159	  Every finite real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix is the Gram matrix of
160	  vectors in a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space. When its entries are
161	  nonnegative, the value $\mathscr{S}(C)$ is independent of its realization.
162	\end{lemma}
163	
164	\begin{proof}
165	  Induct on the size, with the empty matrix realized in $\{0\}$. Diagonal
166	  entries are nonnegative. If all vanish, testing on $e_i+t e_j$ gives $2tC_{ij}
167	  \ge 0$ for every real $t$, hence $C = 0$, realized by zero vectors. Otherwise
168	  permute a positive diagonal $c$ into the first position and write $C =
169	  \left[\begin{smallmatrix}c&v^{\mathsf{T}}\\v&A\end{smallmatrix}\right]$. The
170	  Schur complement $B = A-vv^{\mathsf{T}}/c$ is positive semidefinite: test the
171	  original quadratic form on $(-v^{\mathsf{T}}y/c,y)$. Realize $B$ by vectors
172	  $u_i$ using the induction hypothesis. Then $k_1 = (\sqrt c,0)$ and $k_i =
173	  (v_i/\sqrt c,u_i)$ for the other indices realize $C$. Undo the permutation.
174	  Entries of $B$ need not be nonnegative; this construction requires neither
175	  nonnegative coordinates nor complete positivity.
176	
177	  In any realization, $C_{ii} = 0$ means $k_i = 0$, so its entire row vanishes.
178	  Formula~\eqref{E:gram-active-duality} depends only on $C,\ell,b$ and these
179	  eligible indices. It therefore proves realization independence whenever the
180	  entries are nonnegative, which is the scope in which $\mathscr{S}(C)$ is used.
181	  This proves Lemma~\ref{L:gram-realization}.
182	\end{proof}
183	
184	\begin{proposition}[Entrywise Gram comparison]\label{P:gram-entrywise-comparison}
185	  Let $C,D$ be real symmetric positive semidefinite matrices on the same finite
186	  index set, with $0 \le C_{ij} \le D_{ij}$. With the same $\ell_i > 0,b_i \ge
187	  0$,
188	  \[
189	    \mathscr{S}(C)\le\mathscr{S}(D).
190	  \]
191	  No positive-semidefinite order on $D-C$ is required.
192	\end{proposition}
193	
194	\begin{proof}
195	  Lemma~\ref{L:gram-realization} defines both values. Their eligible sets
196	  satisfy $\mathcal{J}_C \subset \mathcal{J}_D$. For nonempty $A \subset
197	  \mathcal{J}_C$ and positive weights,
198	  \[
199	    D_A^D(w)-D_A^C(w)

559	\begin{lemma}[The physical two-point integral]\label{L:spatial-physical-pair}
560	  The positive measure $\nu(\ud x,\ud y) = \ud x\,\Gamma(\ud y)$ is
561	  sigma-finite. For nonnegative functions define
562	  \begin{equation}\label{E:spatial-physical-pair}
563	    B_\Gamma(f,h)=\int f(x)h(x-y)\nu(\ud x,\ud y)
564	  \end{equation}

566	  representatives of Lebesgue classes. Its value is representative independent.
567	  Lebesgue-a.e. convergence transfers to $\nu$-a.e. convergence at both
568	  positions $x$ and $x-y$.

573	  Lebesgue measure is sigma-finite. If $N$ is Borel and Lebesgue null, Tonelli
574	  applied first in $x$ gives $\nu\{x\in N\} = 0$ and $\nu\{x-y\in N\} = 0$,

576	  has a Borel null superset. Thus, arbitrary versions are measurable in the
577	  $\nu$ completion with the same value, and the same observation applies to the
578	  exceptional sets of a.e. convergence. Signed pairings will be used only after

1022	  \end{equation}

1024	  exponents $m$ and $m/(m-1)$, $m > 1$. If $Z \ge 0$ has finite expectation $F$
